text: Cassini is old and running low on fuel. At the end, they guided it into Saturn's atmosphere so it would burn up. If it had been left adrift, it could have drifted into a moon like Enceladus, where liquid water and organic chemistry make it interesting. The worry is that microbes from Earth on the spacecraft could spread to a moon that might already have life. Crashing into Saturn destroys the probe cleanly. I always thought that was the better ending. It is also easier on Saturn's rings. A controlled plunge beats the messy option of floating around for years.

Your still leg hurts because it is doing the quiet work nobody notices. It holds most of your body weight, keeps the board from tipping, and absorbs every bump, crack and dip in the pavement. Pushing the ground is what gets attention, but the leg left on the board is the one that stays loaded for the whole ride. I've found that the soreness usually comes after a session, not during it, and it's often in the knee, the outer thigh, or the calf. That's because the leg is bracing, not relaxing. If you lean to the board side, that leg has to work even harder to stop the board swinging out. A stiff knee or a tucked stance will make the pain worse, and a rider who pushes too hard with one leg can put extra twist on the standing leg. On a bumpy street, the still leg takes every vibration straight into the knee and hip. The board's tail can also slap your foot, or the ground can pull it sideways. If you keep one foot planted too long, the muscles get cramped. I've noticed that when the pavement is rough, I feel it in the ankle and lower leg, not the thigh. Warm up before you go, keep your knees bent, and try to distribute your weight evenly. But if the pain keeps coming back after normal riding, or you get it with only a short ride, then it's worth checking how you're standing. Sometimes a small change in how your foot sits on the deck makes a big difference. Your pushing leg gets tired in a different way, but the board leg is the one doing the constant holding. The pushing leg gets the credit for moving you, but the stationary leg is carrying the real load.

It's not a passport issue. A lot of Black Americans were born in the US, and many don't live in Africa, but the label points to ancestry. Most Black people in the US trace family roots to places like West and Central Africa, even if the family came generations ago. That connection is what makes the name make sense. I find it confusing too when people hear "African American" and picture someone from Ghana or Nigeria. The term also gets used loosely, and it can sweep in people from the Caribbean, Brazil, or Asia. In that loose use, "African American" becomes a broad umbrella rather than a claim that anyone is from Africa right now. I'd call it an imperfect label, but it isn't trying to say every Black person currently lives in Africa. The ancestry angle is the main reason it's used. I've seen it on forms and school materials, and it always bugged me a little. A Black person from Brooklyn isn't necessarily from Lagos or Accra. But many families kept stories, names, and customs that go back across the Atlantic. That's the part people miss. The word isn't saying anyone is currently from Africa. It points to the old roots.

Mostly they come in through the country's borders: sea, road, air. Russia has supplied government forces for years, and Iran and Hezbollah have helped too. Many armed groups have local workshops and capture weapons from fallen fighters. They keep getting them because the war made weapons a normal part of daily life. Local militias use guns to defend neighborhoods, control checkpoints, and collect fees. Some leaders treat weapons as a way to show power, fund their groups, and keep factions in line. Once a community is armed, it's hard to put the guns back in a safe.

The way I see it, “bad” here mostly means the body adapts to the drug and then reacts badly when it isn't there. With heroine and coke, the intense high is not some separate feature bolted on top. It is the reward system getting flooded. The same flooding makes the brain dial itself down, and that dial-down is what people feel as craving and withdrawal.

I know people who do coke in the afternoon and then can't sleep for days. I know a guy who takes heroin every morning and feels fine until the morning wears off and his hands start shaking. I've seen this enough that I don't treat “no adverse effects” as impossible. A drug with zero bad effects would still have to touch the same reward circuits that create the euphoria. If it does, the brain adapts. Tolerance builds. You need more of the drug to get the same feeling. The good effect and the bad effect come from the same place.

I keep coming back to that. For heroine and coke, the intense pleasure isn't a side product. It's the main thing the drug does. The brain doesn't stay unchanged because of that. It recalibrates. That's why most people who use those drugs end up needing more. I'm not saying all drugs are bad for everyone. Some people use them casually and manage. But the question of “zero adverse effects” trips me up. If a drug could spike reward without touching the same pathways, sure. But that's a different drug than heroine or coke. For those two, the euphoria and the adaptation are one thing. The reason people say drugs are “bad” is that the good part comes with the cost.

I know a woman who takes a few tablets of ecstasy at a weekend party. She says the high lasts only a few hours, but the sleepiness after it can last a day or two. I've had caffeine and green tea in the morning. The first half hour feels bright. The headache after it is a different story. Those aren't zero adverse effects. There's also the physical toll. Heroin slows breathing, drops blood pressure, and makes the body lean on the drug. Coke raises the heart rate, spikes blood pressure, and leaves people jittery. Neither is a drug with zero adverse effects. The intense euphoria comes with these body changes. You can take the drug and feel fine for a while, but the body keeps keeping score. I've watched someone do that with alcohol. The hangover comes in the morning. The drug and the aftereffects are hard to split.

I've been thinking about this after seeing the same tradeoff described again. The pleasure is the hook. The brain changes around it. You can't get the intense high without the high also changing what normal feels like. That's the bit that makes “zero adverse effects” feel like a fantasy. For heroine, coke, and the others, the good feeling and the bad feelings are tied together.

Hi,
I don't think it's a regular headache. A long shopping day can give you a tension headache. The strain of carrying bags, standing, and being in a crowd can tighten your neck and shoulders. That can make your scalp feel pressed tight. Not drinking water or skipping food will add to it. I'd stretch my neck and drink water when I get that feel. The mall is bright and loud, and that can make the pressure worse. Take a walk outside for a minute and let your head settle. If it keeps following you home, see a doctor.
Best,
Alex

Hi,

Thanks for sending this. What happened was a word slip, not a wrong idea about cows. When he asked, your mind jumped to milk because milk is the strongest word tied to cows. That word sat in the answer slot. Cows drink water. Milk is the product. You said milk first, then caught it. The question came right after the silk and spelling game. It's pretty normal for the first association to win. You're not losing it. I've had the same thing happen, and it passes when I say it out loud again. Don't worry about it. You know the answer is water. That's not what you said. The first word won the race in your head. It doesn't mean anything is wrong. I make the same mistake sometimes. Your brain had already heard silk five times. It left extra junk in the answer lane.

Best,
Me

Hi there,
Thanks for sending the house-buying questions. You didn't include the actual questions in your email, so I'll cover the bits that trip people up.

If you're asking about budgeting, the biggest cost people miss is that the purchase price is not the total. Add stamp duty, legal fees, survey costs. If you're asking about mortgages, don't assume the first lender offer is best; compare a few brokers or direct offers. If it's about surveys, a basic survey may miss defects, but a full structural survey is better for older or non-standard homes. If you're asking what to look at during viewings, check damp, window seals, plumbing, and any signs of previous leaks. If it's about timing, buying when your budget is firm helps, and don't rush because you've seen one house.

For older houses, I'd get a full survey rather than the basic one. A surveyor can flag things you can't see, like old wiring or cracked foundations. Don't ignore the neighbourhood; traffic and parking matter more than glossy photos. Keep your documents together: ID, payslips, and a list of open questions for the seller.

Send me the exact questions and I can be more specific.

Thanks,
Sam

Hi Sam,

The short version is that a 3-in-1 has to clean skin and hair in the same formula, so the mix of surfactants, oils and conditioning agents gets adjusted for both jobs. A shampoo/conditioner is tuned mostly for hair. Add the bodywash part, and it tends to have more general skin-cleaning ingredients, which can make the lather feel different on the arms and legs.

For me the real difference is convenience more than performance. I use the 3-in-1 in the shower when I'm in a hurry. It saves a bottle on the shelf, but I still keep a proper bodywash and a proper shampoo for most days. The 2-in-1 I tried once, and it felt like it was doing both jobs halfway.

So if you're deciding which one to buy, the 3-in-1 is the all-in-one shortcut; the 2-in-1 is a hair-specific combo. That's about it.

Best,
Riley

Hey Sam,

They put GPS receivers on the landmass and compare positions over a year or more. The markers are little concrete pillars in fields or bolted to buildings. The change in position gives a speed, usually a few millimetres a year. I found that part pretty straightforward. You can't feel it day to day, so the GPS markers are the only way to see it. The plates are moving, but slowly, so you need years of data. I always thought the continents were still, but the numbers show a constant slow drift. The receivers are weatherproof boxes with antennas on top, and their positions are checked against a global reference. Someone walks the markers once a year and collects the data. It's a boring but reliable way to do it. It's not something you can see with your eyes. I'd say the GPS part is the main answer. The satellite part is the backup. Radar satellites pass over and measure tiny ground shifts with InSAR. That catches motion in areas with subsidence or active faulting. The numbers come out in mm/year, and you can map them across the whole plate. The radar helps fill gaps where it's hard to place stations.

Best,
Alex

Inbreeding makes it more likely that a child gets the same hidden defect from both parents. Most people carry a few rare gene changes that don't show unless two matching copies meet. When relatives mate, those hidden copies are more likely to match because they share ancestors. For IQ, the relevant changes usually touch brain development, language, learning, or basic cognition. A child with two bad copies of such a gene can show lower cognitive ability, though most children with inbred parents do not automatically have low IQ. I'd treat IQ as only one visible sign, not the whole problem. The science is that harmful combinations become more common in the next generation. These effects are usually subtle across a population, but a specific bad gene pair can cause a clear drop in a child's test scores. It is not a simple cause-and-effect, but a changed probability of hidden defects.

It can feel like an arm injury hurts less, but that is not universal. I've noticed that an injury to the arm seems less intense than one to the torso or head, especially when the wound is shallow. That does not mean it is painless.

The upper arm and forearm have more fat, muscle, and room to move. A hit, shot, or stab in the arm is spread through thicker soft tissue, and the arm can flex away from the injury. My own experience is that forearm wounds sting and throb, but they do not lock me up the way a rib or knee injury does. The skin on the arm is not as dense with nerve endings as the face, back of the hand, or feet. Also, we often guard the limb, which changes how we describe the pain. Still, a deep cut in the arm can be brutal.

Carbon monoxide is the one I'd watch first. It is colorless and odorless, and it lingers in rooms where engines or heaters have run. It is not a normal body gas. It grabs onto hemoglobin in red blood cells far more tightly than oxygen does. Oxygen has a hard time replacing it. Your blood then carries less oxygen to your heart, brain, and muscles. You can get sick slowly, with headache, dizziness, or sleepiness, before you realize anything is wrong.

Carbon dioxide is something the body makes all the time. You breathe it out. Small amounts in air are normal. It only becomes a problem when it builds up to very high levels, as in a sealed room or a big greenhouse. The body senses high carbon dioxide and makes you breathe faster. It can make you feel warm, dizzy, or tired.

I'd skip the idea that one is harmless and the other deadly. That is too neat. Carbon dioxide has limits. Carbon monoxide is the sneaky one. You can't smell it. It binds where oxygen should be. A room that smells fine can still have invisible danger. If a heater or car is running and the window is closed, carbon monoxide can collect in a quiet room. If someone else in the room feels the same, it is worth getting out and getting fresh air.

I've seen this in places people assume are safe. A garage with a car running, a kitchen with a stove in use, a workshop with a generator in the corner. The air can feel normal. Your head may ache before you connect it to the room. Fresh air is the easy fix. Open a door, step outside, or move the source of heat or fuel out of the room.

The brace position is a safety posture for sudden impacts in an aircraft. It protects your head, neck, back, legs, and feet. When a plane stops quickly, your body keeps moving. Your arms hold your head to the headrest or a pillow. Your knees stay together. Your feet stay flat on the floor. Your seat belt stays tight. This keeps your body in one fixed shape. The second impact, where your body hits the seat, tray, or floor, is what bracing helps reduce. I think of it as a plain posture you practice until it feels automatic. I have seen flight crews emphasize it during water landings and hard landings. The posture does not stop the aircraft from slowing. It stops you from becoming loose inside the cabin.

In most cabins you can do this while seated. You bend forward. Your head goes to the headrest. Your arms cross over your lap or your stomach. Your feet press down on the floor. If you are standing, you lean toward the cabin wall and keep your feet apart. The point is not to look dramatic. It is to keep your body from hitting things hard.

Most old trading houses and guild workshops closed long before the machines arrived. When a founder died, the shop usually went under and the name was not strong enough to survive on its own. I always find it hard to believe that, because we talk about brands as if they last forever. The industrial era changed what people expected from shops. Old names got swallowed up by bigger factories, and their signs vanished from streets. A shop could be famous in a city, but once the owners stopped running it, the story ends. I think the missing examples are not mysterious.

I still think the dealer's lower rate is the cheapest way to borrow only if every dollar of the loan buys the car you wanted at a fair price. In my experience, the lower dealer rate comes bundled with a higher price. The car you test drive gets a new sticker with accessories, paint protection, or service plans added before you sit down to finance. The lower interest rate then applies to a bigger number. The bank quote I use is a little higher, but I know exactly what I am borrowing and how much I will pay each month.

Dealership financing also tends to pull you into the dealer's world. A lower advertised rate can come with a required service plan, roadside coverage, or an extended warranty you did not ask for. If you accept them, your monthly cost goes up. I have watched a salesperson add a few hundred dollars for extras and still hand you a lower rate. The rate is the easy part. The hard part is that the loan amount includes everything the dealer wanted to sell, not just the vehicle.

A bank can be cheaper when you already know the car's price. You bring an outside quote and compare it against the dealer's total monthly payment, not just the rate. I would rather pay a slightly higher rate on a smaller loan than accept a lower rate on a loan padded with dealer extras.

The point is not that one lender always beats the other. A lower interest rate is only useful if the principal is fair. If the dealership raises the sale price to fund the discount, you pay for the discount over and over again. I have seen a car quoted lower with a dealer loan, but after fees and extras the total was higher than the same car financed at a bank.

My position is simple: check the final amount financed and the monthly payment. If the dealership's lower rate is attached to a higher price, a bank can win on total cost. I would not sign a dealer deal without a side-by-side of bank and dealer terms. I ask for a printed quote before I sign anything, and I read the fee lines twice. The expensive part is what the dealer decides to include before you sign. That is why I compare the final bill, not just the interest line.

I've always found the patchwork of marijuana laws confusing. One state lets you grow six plants in your garage, another treats the same plants like evidence of a crime. For me, that gap feels like a small, ordinary frustration you run into everywhere: I can buy a bud pack in Denver but get pulled over in Columbus for the smell. I think more states should allow adults to use it legally. People should know which box they're standing in before they light up. My neighbor in Portland grows a few small pots on her patio, and nobody says anything. My cousin in Boise keeps hers under the kitchen table. Same plant, same green smell, two different answers. The states are testing the waters. It isn't just a legal line. It changes how people carry it around. I want that testing to stop treating a common adult choice like a hidden mistake.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the body doesn't make electricity in a power plant. Each cell keeps a voltage difference across its membrane by moving sodium and potassium in and out. When a signal travels down a nerve, tiny gaps along the nerve briefly reverse that charge, like a row of dominoes. I imagine my arm as wires and switches, and the muscles are where the signal becomes visible. I take the position that body electricity is just chemistry carrying charge. The heart is the clearest example, because its cells fire themselves and keep the rhythm.

Most musicians sample older songs by isolating a small piece of a track and turning it into a loop. I have watched this happen in a bedroom studio at my friend’s apartment. She put a scratched CD through the soundcard, selected a few seconds of a piano line, and dragged it into Ableton. The piano loop became the base for a new beat. She changed the pitch and added a kick under it. The keyboard keys were sticky, and the speakers were old. The room smelled like coffee and dust. I keep a folder of loops I cut myself. Some came from CDs that fell apart. Some came from friends’ playlists. I use a small pair of studio headphones and a secondhand laptop. The desk was covered in paper and a glass of tea.

I think sampling is less about writing a new song and more about finding the one piece of an old song that already works. A producer can lift a drum break, a vocal chop, or a bass figure and build a track around it. The old song gives the new one its character.

There is a line between using a snippet and copying the whole thing. If a producer takes a short piano riff and makes it the center of a track, the original author usually gets a share. If a producer changes the sound with filters and effects until it is hard to place, the line moves. I find that line useful. It lets new artists borrow an old groove without buying the whole song. My friend calls it borrowing a flavor, not stealing a whole cake. I mostly agree.

A short piano loop from an old soul record can be the soul of a new hip-hop track. The older song gives the new one a smell and a feel. I have sat through enough sessions to know that cleanup takes patience. A good sample does not sound glued on. It sits in the mix like a familiar face in a new crowd.

My position is simple. Sampling older songs is a way to keep old music alive without making it museum glass. It gives new writers a shortcut into a known groove. I would rather hear a clean, short piece of the old song than a copy of it. If the sample still makes me want to dance, it has done its job.

My head doesn't ache because something is wrong. I think it's because the blood vessels near my scalp and temples tighten, and the nerves around them fire. When I skip lunch, my scalp gets hot, my temples throb, and I can feel that tight ring around my head. It's not magic; it's pressure and nerve signals. I press the sides of my temples with two fingers and sometimes it feels like I'm pressing on an angry knot. I've learned to look at my own pattern: stress and skipped meals are my usual triggers. I don't chase science. For me, a headache is a small alarm that my body is asking for water, food, or rest. The pain is real, but it doesn't always mean danger. I keep a glass of water and a sandwich nearby, and most days the throb eases. It's less scary when I stop treating it like a mystery.

I can't tell you if the food is good. We never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We picked this spot because we had a 10 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We put our names on their useless digital waitlist. They told us to come back at 8:23 p.m. to pay. We came back. We stood around until 8:40 p.m. Then a worker casually said we might not get a table until 9:15. It was just a party of two. No solutions. If the wait stretches that far after paying, say so upfront. Otherwise people waste their night. A disaster. If zero stars were an option, I'd give it zero.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. There were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. If the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Three and a half stars. The space bar rattles. I hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself. They were brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up. I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well the under-21 version, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and I really found it mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re looking down into it, so from almost any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, like the strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, but if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, too much was happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on each other. A more restrained production would have hit harder. It felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle, where more is treated as better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t really expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. The shirts never came. The sales rep got the address wrong. Her written seven was read as one. We meant 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people living at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to send it back. After that, the package disappeared. We didn't learn until several weeks later. In the middle of the argument over it, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount said no refund on the first two. The owner handled it at that stage. He admitted the package went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts came back. He also said it was partly our fault because we hadn't been friendly enough to the people at 5401, four doors away. That really annoyed us. We disputed the original charge with our credit card company. We eventually got the credit.
